title: Myofascial pain in older adults: a geroscience-informed framework integrating precision geriatrics and digital therapeutics
authors: Chang Zhu; Jie Xu; Yating Gong; Chaoyu Wang; Wenting Xu; Lijun Chen
pain_condition_detail: Myofascial pain syndrome (MPS) in older adults; related chronic musculoskeletal pain and chronic low back pain.
context_note: Older adults in community, long-term care, primary/geriatric clinics, and Chinese/resource-limited settings; U.S. prevalence cited.
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The model is operationalized as a clinician-facing review framework: age-specific pathophysiology, precision diagnostics, pharmacology/de-prescribing, non-pharmacological interventions, psychological therapies, and multidisciplinary care. It defines BPS pain as peripheral nociception, central processing, and psychological state, then maps interventions to those domains rather than testing a three-domain causal model.
integration_mechanism_summary: The strongest pathway is biological: aging-related tissue and inflammatory changes produce central sensitization, which psychological factors top-down modulate. Social factors mainly alter access to psychological care and multidisciplinary implementation; no full three-domain causal mechanism is specified.
conceptual_tensions_1: MPS is framed both as a localized myofascial condition with trigger points and as a complex geriatric syndrome rooted in aging biology
conceptual_tensions_2: The review advocates a geroscience-informed mechanistic cascade but states that interactions among aging mechanisms remain largely theoretical
conceptual_tensions_3: Digital therapeutics are promoted for access, while the digital divide is identified as a barrier to equitable uptake
conceptual_tensions_4: Multidisciplinary care is idealized, but the case example shows missing psychology and social work in China/resource-limited settings
conceptual_tensions_5: Non-pharmacological care is prioritized, but pharmacological precision prescribing and de-prescribing remain necessary
additional_observations_1: The review prioritizes high-quality evidence but uses a narrative thematic synthesis, not a pooled meta-analysis or formal systematic review
additional_observations_2: The social domain is mostly implementation/access: digital divide, family support, social determinants, and care-team composition
additional_observations_3: The clinical case is used rhetorically and illustratively, not analyzed as empirical data
additional_observations_4: Several citation placeholders are blank in the supplied text, so attribution is sometimes unresolvable
additional_observations_5: The framework is actionable for clinicians but not empirically validated as a model
synthesis_note: This narrative review operationalizes BPS as a clinician-facing multimodal framework for geriatric MPS. Biological geroscience mechanisms are the strongest thread; psychological constructs and therapies are integrated mechanistically with central sensitization; social factors enter mainly as access, support, and care-system gaps. It offers descriptive triadic integration but few tested cross-domain pathways.
coding_rationale: Biological and psychological content are elaborated; social content is mentioned. Bio-psych integration is mechanistic, triadic integration descriptive. Typology true_integrative despite thin social domain.
biological_factors_01_factor_verbatim: Sarcopenia, the age-related loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength, is a cornerstone of this decline. Beginning in the fourth decade of life, muscle mass decreases by approximately 8% per decade, accelerating after the age of 70. In MPS, sarcopenia creates a vulnerable substrate.
biological_factors_02_factor_verbatim: This leads to fascial stiffening, reduced tissue compliance, and impaired gliding between fascial layers. This increased stiffness can directly contribute to pain by compressing embedded nociceptors and small nerve fibers.
biological_factors_03_factor_verbatim: Underpinning these changes is profound mitochondrial dysfunction. Aging muscle is characterized by a decline in mitochondrial biogenesis, reduced efficiency of the electron transport chain, and an accumulation of mitochondrial DNA mutations.
biological_factors_04_factor_verbatim: Superimposed on these structural changes is a systemic, pro-inflammatory state known as “inflammaging.” This refers to the chronic, low-grade, sterile inflammation that characterizes the aging process.
biological_factors_05_factor_label: cellular senescence and the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP)
biological_factors_05_factor_verbatim: A key driver of inflammaging is cellular senescence—the accumulation of non-dividing but metabolically active cells that secrete a cocktail of inflammatory mediators, known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP).
biological_factors_06_factor_verbatim: In many older adults with chronic MPS, the pain experience is no longer solely driven by the peripheral MTrP. The constant barrage of nociceptive signals from the dysfunctional muscle tissue leads to profound neuroplastic changes in the central nervous system (CNS), a process known as central sensitization.
biological_factors_07_factor_label: neuroendocrine dysregulation and the HPA axis
biological_factors_07_factor_verbatim: Age-related changes in the neuroendocrine system also play a crucial role. Dysregulation of the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis, the body’s central stress response system, is common in older adults.
biological_factors_08_factor_verbatim: For instance, a high prevalence of vitamin D deficiency has been observed in patients with chronic MPS, with age and limited sun exposure being significant risk factors.
biological_factors_09_factor_verbatim: Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs): While effective for acute inflammatory pain, the chronic use of NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen, naproxen) is strongly discouraged in the elderly.
biological_factors_10_factor_verbatim: Gabapentinoids (Gabapentin and Pregabalin): These drugs are widely prescribed for neuropathic pain, but their efficacy in nociceptive or mixed pain states like MPS is limited.
biological_factors_11_factor_verbatim: Selective Sodium Channel Blockers: A highly promising frontier is the development of selective inhibitors of the NaV1.8 sodium channel.
biological_factors_12_factor_verbatim: A pharmacological frontier with particular relevance to geriatric MPS is senolytic therapy—agents designed to selectively eliminate senescent cells that accumulate with aging and drive chronic inflammation through the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP).

title: Acceptance of pain neuroscience education in chronic musculoskeletal pain conditions: qualitative systematic review
authors: Lukas Kühn; Eileen Wengemuth; Lara Kleist; Kyung Eun (Anna) Choi
pain_condition_detail: Chronic musculoskeletal pain conditions, including chronic low back pain, fibromyalgia, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, neck pain, gout, and chronic fatigue syndrome.
context_note: Included studies came from England, New Zealand, Australia, the United States, the Netherlands, Portugal, and Lebanon; settings were primary, secondary, or tertiary musculoskeletal care.
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; operational definition; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper operationalizes BPS mainly as the content and scope of PNE: education about pain origins, biopsychosocial etiology, and biological mechanisms. Acceptance is organized around patient beliefs, relevance, setting, clinician relationship, provider confidence, and role clarity. Domains are mostly listed as determinants, not modeled as interacting mechanisms.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper specifies some pathways: trust toward clinicians reduces pain-related neural activity and can support engagement/learning; group settings provide support that may enhance motivation/adherence; PNE biological content is expected to change pain beliefs/behaviours. No triadic mechanism is specified.
quality_assessment_tools_1: jbi critical appraisal tool for qualitative research
emergent_labels_9: professional culture focused on biomedical aspects of care
conceptual_tensions_1: PNE is framed as biopsychosocial, but much of the operational content is biological pain education, so social and psychological domains enter mainly as determinants of acceptance
conceptual_tensions_2: Brain-based pain explanations may reduce tissue-damage beliefs, yet the review reports they can make pain seem invented or psychological
conceptual_tensions_3: Clinicians recognize psychological factors, but the paper finds limited tools, confidence, training, and professional culture barriers to addressing them
conceptual_tensions_4: Group PNE is described as motivating and supportive, but also potentially tiring, hard to remember, and not suitable for all patients
conceptual_tensions_5: The paper calls for mechanistic work on clinician–patient relationship, but explicitly notes a lack of experimental evidence for that relationship
additional_observations_1: The review is not a direct test of BPS as a model, it is a review of determinants of PNE acceptance
additional_observations_2: The BPS label appears in inclusion criteria, but the synthesis organizes findings as facilitators/barriers rather than as domains with specified interactions
additional_observations_3: Included studies were adult chronic musculoskeletal pain patients and healthcare providers from multiple countries and care levels
additional_observations_4: The review excludes pediatric, postsurgical, cancer-related, and pregnancy-related chronic pain
additional_observations_5: PNE variants include video, booklets, metaphors, in-person sessions, group sessions, individualized sessions, and multimodal PNE+
additional_observations_6: The paper relies heavily on qualitative determinants and cites experimental evidence only selectively in the discussion
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS mainly as the content and scope of PNE rather than as a tested explanatory model. Biological and psychological material is central; social factors are mostly implementation determinants. It lists domains and determinants, but does not model a three-domain mechanism.
coding_rationale: BPS is used as an organizing/operational frame for PNE; all three domains appear, but mainly as parallel determinants of acceptance. Mechanistic pairwise links are noted, especially trust–neural activity, so triadic integration is partial.

citation: Smits et al. (2026), Osteoarthritis and Cartilage Open
title: Biopsychosocial predictive factors for developing chronic postsurgical pain after hip replacement surgery: A systematic review
authors: Rachel J.H. Smits; Rosa Poppen; Jetze Visser; Kris C.P. Vissers; Selina E.I. van der Wal
pain_condition_detail: Chronic postsurgical pain after total hip arthroplasty for end-stage osteoarthritis.
context_note: Worldwide increase in total hip arthroplasties; no country-specific healthcare-system context reported.
bps_function_set: conclusion; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; justification; operational definition; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The review operationalizes BPS through eligibility and extraction of preoperative patient-related biopsychosocial/economic predictors, then organizes results into biological, socioeconomic, and psychological sections. It uses BPS to justify prehabilitation, multimodal analgesia, and informed consent, but does not define the model or specify cross-domain mechanisms.
integration_mechanism_summary: No detailed cross-domain mechanism is proposed. The paper asserts directional links, notes possible coping/social-support mechanisms, and reports that neuropathic-like pain associations may be explained by central sensitization and catastrophizing.
quality_assessment_tools_3: grading of recommendations assessment, development and evaluation (grade)
emergent_labels_10: Quadratus lumborum of Pericapsular Nerve Group block
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper uses a broad BPS frame while not defining the model itself
conceptual_tensions_2: Biological and psychological evidence is detailed, but socioeconomic evidence rests mainly on one education study
conceptual_tensions_3: Pain sensitization, neuropathic-like pain, and catastrophizing overlap, and adjustment changes associations
conceptual_tensions_4: Many reported associations are inconsistent across observational studies
conceptual_tensions_5: Clinical implications extend to preoperative opioid reduction and digital adherence support even though some were excluded or not included
additional_observations_1: Meta-analysis was not conducted because of heterogeneity and limited studies per category
additional_observations_2: All included studies were observational cohort designs, resulting in low overall quality
additional_observations_3: The review distinguishes modifiable from non-modifiable risk factors for prehabilitation and informed consent
additional_observations_4: Some included studies also included knee or shoulder arthroplasty but required separate THA data
additional_observations_5: The paper uses 'biopsychosocial' to organize risk-factor extraction and clinical recommendations rather than to define variables in a single predictive model
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS as a structured inventory of preoperative predictors for CPSP after THA. Biological and psychological factors are developed in detail; socioeconomic factors are mentioned but evidence is thin; lifestyle implications are added in discussion. It proposes no cross-domain mechanism and mostly links domains as associated risk factors.
coding_rationale: BPS is primarily an organizing/intervention frame. Bio and psych are elaborated, social and lifestyle mentioned, spiritual absent. Triadic integration is descriptive, not mechanistic.

title: Self‐Management Therapies for Temporomandibular Disorders—Evidence From Systematic Reviews
authors: Tessa Bijelic; Ambrosina Michelotti; Rosaria Bucci; Daniela Del Sorbo; EwaCarin Ekberg; Birgitta Häggman‐Henrikson
icd11_pain_category: chronic secondary headache or orofacial pain
pain_condition_detail: Temporomandibular disorders (TMD), described as orofacial pain involving masticatory muscles and temporomandibular joints.
context_note: Included SRs were conducted in the United Kingdom, Brazil, Canada, China, Germany, Italy, and Japan.
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; justification; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: The review uses BPS mainly as a justification for patient-centred, multimodal self-management. It operationalizes BPS through intervention components (patient education, behavioural/CBT, jaw exercises) and outcomes (pain, mouth opening, quality of life), with no explicit three-domain mechanism.
integration_mechanism_summary: One behavioural mechanism is proposed: behavioural therapy is said to target jaw-system rehabilitation by identifying, monitoring and avoiding disadvantageous behaviours and reinforcing advantageous behaviours. No explicit three-domain mechanism is proposed.
emergent_labels_10: disc displacement with or without reduction
conceptual_tensions_1: BPS language is used to support self-management, but the paper does not turn the model into measured variables or a triadic mechanism
conceptual_tensions_2: Self-management is described as multimodal, yet the heterogeneity of components makes it difficult to attribute effects to specific parts
conceptual_tensions_3: Evidence is reported as beneficial, but certainty is often low or very low and methodological concerns are frequent
conceptual_tensions_4: Patient education, behavioural therapy and CBT are sometimes grouped as psychological interventions, creating conceptual overlap
conceptual_tensions_5: Quality of life and adverse effects are recommended as important outcomes but are less often reported in the included reviews
additional_observations_1: No psychological instruments are named for constructs such as kinesiophobia, pain catastrophising, coping or CBT outcomes
additional_observations_2: DC/TMD and RDC/TMD are used as diagnostic classification systems, not as measures of biopsychosocial constructs
additional_observations_3: Included systematic reviews were conducted in seven countries, but no country-specific social mechanisms are analysed
additional_observations_4: The paper does not name family, cultural, socioeconomic, compensation, stigma, or social determinant factors
additional_observations_5: Future research recommendations emphasize children and adolescents, quality of life, and adverse effects
additional_observations_6: The review reports 53% overlap of primary studies across included systematic reviews
synthesis_note: The paper uses BPS mainly to justify patient-centred, multimodal self-management for TMD. Biological content is mostly TMD anatomy, pain/function outcomes and jaw exercises; psychological content is education/behavioural/CBT and related constructs. Social content is limited to demographics, healthcare professionals and patient-centred framing. It does not propose a three-domain mechanism.
coding_rationale: Multifactorial typology: all domains appear, but social content is thin and cross-domain claims are mostly intervention-based rather than mechanistic.

citation: Han et al. (2026), Frontiers in Pain Research
title: Chronic pain in transgender and gender-diverse youth: a biopsychosocial perspective
authors: Gloria T. Han; Molly Basch; Diane Chen; Lonnie Zeltzer
pain_condition_detail: Chronic primary pain including headaches, widespread musculoskeletal pain, and abdominal pain, plus chronic secondary pain associated with other health conditions in transgender and gender-diverse youth.
context_note: United States, Canada, and Sweden are cited for prevalence, identity estimates, and school-based pain data; policy stressors are described as a U.S. patchwork.
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The review uses biopsychosocial language as an organizing and explanatory frame, structuring content around neurobiological vulnerabilities, psychosocial distress, and societal/systemic barriers. It does not operationalize BPS into measured variables; it synthesizes mechanisms and care implications.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes several pathways: minority stress and discrimination affect HPA-axis dysregulation, cortisol, inflammation, and central sensitization; anxiety/depression amplify pain sensitivity through shared neural circuits; gender dysphoria increases bodily vigilance and avoidance behaviors; gender-affirming care may reduce distress and stigma, buffering pain-exacerbating physiological and psychological processes.
bps_model_variants_3: biopsychosocial conceptualizations and models of care
conceptual_tensions_1: The review treats chronic primary and chronic secondary pain together while also noting that mechanisms and contextual challenges may differ across the two
conceptual_tensions_2: The paper emphasizes social and systemic determinants but states that evidence on many proposed mechanisms remains limited or indirect
conceptual_tensions_3: Gender-affirming care is framed as potentially protective while some practices such as chest binding, tucking, packing, and voice training are also described as capable of causing localized pain or strain
conceptual_tensions_4: The review calls for longitudinal and mechanistic research because direct chronic pain endpoints have not been studied for pubertal suppression or subsequent GAHT
conceptual_tensions_5: Intersex youth are conceptually relevant to sex characteristics and gender diversity but are explicitly outside the review's scope
additional_observations_1: The review's BPS operationalization is primarily narrative synthesis and clinical framing rather than a coded or measured BPS framework
additional_observations_2: The review cites mechanisms such as central sensitization, HPA-axis dysregulation, inflammatory processes, and shared neural circuits as cross-domain bridges
additional_observations_3: The paper includes lifestyle behaviors only as consequences of gender dysphoria-related avoidance, not as a developed lifestyle domain
additional_observations_4: Spiritual or existential content appears only within an intersectional list of systems shaping stress and resources
additional_observations_5: The paper uses the BPS label both analytically and rhetorically, especially in the conclusion where it recommends biopsychosocial care
synthesis_note: This narrative review uses biopsychosocial framing to organize chronic pain in transgender and gender-diverse youth around neurobiological vulnerabilities, psychosocial distress, and societal/systemic barriers. It proposes multiple cross-domain mechanisms, especially through minority stress, HPA-axis dysregulation, inflammation, and central sensitization, but it does not operationalize BPS into measured constructs or a formal model.
coding_rationale: All three core domains are elaborated and linked through stress physiology, pain sensitivity, and care barriers; lifestyle and spiritual content are mentioned only briefly. The typology is true_integrative because the paper relates all domains, though not with a fully specified unified mechanism.

integration_mechanism_summary: Psychosocial factors can set or alter CNS plasticity, descending modulation, nociceptive pathways, and musculoskeletal tissue properties; genetic and epigenetic factors modify these processes; favorable or adverse mixes set adaptive or maladaptive CNS states and sensorimotor outcomes. conceptual_tensions_1: TOPSMI is presented as more comprehensive and mechanistic, yet the authors state it may be difficult to formally test as a whole because many factors are involved
conceptual_tensions_2: The review extends spinal-system evidence to orofacial pain while repeatedly noting that comparable orofacial datasets are much more limited
conceptual_tensions_3: The BPS label brings in sociocultural factors, but the social evidence is thinner than the biological and psychological evidence
conceptual_tensions_4: Management is recommended as customized to individual factor mixtures, but the paper does not provide a formal measurement or coding scheme for those mixtures
conceptual_tensions_5: Prior theories are criticized for lacking a full picture, while TOPSMI is defended as mechanistic despite limited direct testing
additional_observations_1: The paper does not report formal quality assessment or risk-of-bias tools for the evidence it reviews
additional_observations_2: The main operationalization is theoretical: favorable versus adverse mix and weighting of factors sets CNS plasticity state
additional_observations_3: No named psychological instruments, pain outcome instruments, or psychosocial measurement scales are reported
additional_observations_4: The review proposes future longitudinal neuroimaging trials, biopsychosocial stratification, and gene-environment interaction models
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS mainly through TOPSMI rather than through measured constructs. It gives rich biological and psychological mechanisms and a weaker sociocultural layer, so it operationalizes BPS mainly through TOPSMI rather than through measured constructs.
coding_rationale: TOPSMI is mechanistic triadic despite thin social evidence; biological content dominates, and no formal quality/risk tools or instruments are used.

citation: Gromakovskis & Gūtmanis (2025), Journal of Pain Research
title: Flow-Induced Analgesia: A Conceptual Review of Biopsychosocial and Neurobiological Mechanisms of Pain Modulation
authors: Vlodeks Gromakovskis; Mārtiņš Gustavs Gūtmanis
pain_condition_detail: Predominantly chronic and persistent pain, including fibromyalgia, musculoskeletal pain, neuropathic pain, rehabilitation cohorts, and acute experimental pain paradigms.
bps_function_set: explanatory framework; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: Uses BPS as a broad label and FIA as operational mechanism: flow components -> attentional capture, DMN suppression, reward/PFC-striatal-PAG-RVM descending modulation -> analgesia; social content is mainly implementation, not social determinants.
integration_mechanism_summary: Proposed mechanisms: flow -> attentional capture/DMN suppression/reward-PFC-striatal-PAG-RVM/endogenous opioid and endocannabinoid modulation -> analgesia. Flow also -> motivation/adherence/rehabilitation outcomes. Social content is mostly implementation; no full three-domain mechanism is specified.
bps_model_variants_3: biopsychosocial and neurobiological mechanisms of pain modulation
conceptual_tensions_1: The BPS label is used, but the substantive integration is mainly psychological-neurobiological while social content is mostly clinical implementation
conceptual_tensions_2: FIA is proposed as a mechanism, yet the authors repeatedly state that evidence is correlational and causal pathways are unestablished
conceptual_tensions_3: Flow is distinguished from distraction and mindfulness, but it shares attentional and affective features with both
conceptual_tensions_4: Direct flow-pain evidence is sparse, while indirect evidence from VR, music, arts, sports, and rehabilitation is used to support the hypothesis
conceptual_tensions_5: Flow interventions are framed as beneficial, but barriers such as depression, cognitive impairment, low motivation, and excessive immersion are also named
additional_observations_1: Formal quality or bias assessment was not performed, consistent with the conceptual narrative design
additional_observations_2: The review is not a meta-analysis, approximately 40 conceptually relevant studies were qualitatively synthesized
additional_observations_3: Pain conditions are broad and include fibromyalgia, musculoskeletal pain, neuropathic pain, rehabilitation cohorts, and acute experimental pain paradigms
additional_observations_4: The biopsychosocial model is invoked but not formally defined
additional_observations_5: Operationalization occurs mainly through proposed future flow measures rather than measured constructs across all BPS domains
additional_observations_6: Social content centers on access, training, clinics, adherence, and therapeutic alliance rather than socioeconomic, cultural, or structural determinants
synthesis_note: This review uses BPS mainly as a framing label while operationalizing FIA as a psychological-neurobiological pathway. Social content is mostly implementation and access, not social determinants. It offers mechanistic bio-psych links and partial psych-social/bio-social links, but not a true triadic model.
coding_rationale: Dyadic bio-psych focus; social domain is named but thin. FIA proposes mechanisms, yet causal evidence and triadic integration remain limited.
biological_factors_01_factor_verbatim: Functional MRI investigations demonstrate suppression of the DMN, a system associated with self-referential processing and rumination, during flow states.
biological_factors_02_factor_verbatim: Neuroimaging studies have consistently shown that pain perception involves activation of a distributed “pain matrix,” including the insula, anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), thalamus, and prefrontal regions.
biological_factors_03_factor_verbatim: Within this system, the salience network—primarily the anterior insula and dorsal ACC—plays a central role in detecting and prioritizing salient stimuli, including pain.

biological_factors_05_factor_verbatim: At the same time, dopaminergic reward pathways, including the striatum and ventral tegmental area, show increased activity, consistent with the intrinsic reward of flow.
biological_factors_06_factor_verbatim: The striatum interacts with the periaqueductal gray (PAG, red), which participates in descending analgesic pathways mediated by opioidergic and possibly endocannabinoid systems.

psychological_concepts_01_measure_named: Flow State Scale (FSS/FSS-2), Dispositional Flow Scale (DFS), Flow Short Scale (FSS-10), Experience Sampling Method (ESM)
psychological_concepts_01_definition_ver: Flow describes an optimal state of consciousness characterized by total absorption in an activity, a balance between skills and task challenge, diminished self-referential processing, altered sense of time, and intrinsic reward.
psychological_concepts_02_definition_ver: distinguish between trait flow (a dispositional tendency to experience flow) and state flow (a situational, task-induced experience)
psychological_concepts_03_definition_ver: Dispositional flow—an individual’s general tendency to enter flow states—varies widely and may influence treatment response.
psychological_concepts_04_definition_ver: Attention functions as both a gate and an amplifier of pain: selective focus on nociceptive input can heighten distress, whereas diversion of attention may reduce pain perception.
psychological_concepts_05_definition_ver: Pain catastrophizing—defined as an exaggerated negative orientation toward pain stimuli—is a robust predictor of heightened pain intensity, disability, and poor treatment outcomes.
psychological_concepts_06_definition_ver: Hypervigilance compounds this effect: patients focus excessively on somatic sensations, increasing threat appraisal and reinforcing avoidance behaviors.
psychological_concepts_07_definition_ver: Contemporary models highlight the importance of pain-related attention, catastrophizing, hypervigilance, and impaired coping strategies as central determinants of pain intensity and interference.
psychological_concepts_08_definition_ver: Mindfulness-based interventions represent another attentional approach, yet they differ fundamentally from distraction. Rather than diverting attention away from pain, mindfulness involves cultivating nonjudgmental awareness of present-moment experiences, including painful sensations.
psychological_concepts_09_definition_ver: Distraction involves a temporary shift of attention away from pain, which can be passive (eg, watching television) or active (eg, playing a simple game), but it does not necessarily engage intrinsic motivation or deep absorption.
psychological_concepts_10_definition_ver: Flow describes an optimal state of consciousness characterized by deep absorption, intrinsic motivation, and a balance between task challenge and individual skill.
psychological_concepts_11_definition_ver: Flow represents an integration of cognitive, emotional, and motivational processes that creates a sense of effortless concentration, deep engagement, and enjoyment.
psychological_concepts_12_concept_family: emotional regulation and pain affect processing
psychological_concepts_12_definition_ver: Flow elicits positive affect and reduces stress responses, including hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis activation.
psychological_concepts_13_definition_ver: DMN, a system associated with self-referential processing and rumination

title: Is resistance training with external loads superior to unloaded exercise in the management of chronic low back pain? A systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Marco Ranzani; Andrea Pozzi; Daniele Fornasari; Diego Ristori; Marco Testa
pain_condition_detail: Adults with chronic non-specific low back pain (NS-LBP).
context_note: Worldwide prevalence reported; eligible studies restricted to English or Italian language.
bps_function_set: background framing; conclusion; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The review operationalizes BPS mainly by including physical performance outcomes and a few psychosocial measures, then concluding exercise should be individualized and contextually framed; social factors are named but not measured or integrated.
integration_mechanism_summary: Two-domain bio-psych mechanisms are proposed: external load or exercise as graded exposure or behavioral signal to reduce fear, improve confidence and beliefs, and affect pain or disability. Social elements such as context, communication, and therapeutic alliance are acknowledged but not modeled as mechanisms; no full three-domain pathway is specified.
quality_assessment_tools_3: grading of recommendations, assessment, development, and evaluation (grade)
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper uses BPS language to justify individualized care while the actual meta-analysis is dominated by physical outcomes and only a few psychosocial measures
conceptual_tensions_2: External load is theoretically framed as graded exposure, but the included evidence rarely reports psychosocial outcomes and shows no clear psychosocial between-group advantage
conceptual_tensions_3: Clinical interpretation emphasizes meaning, therapeutic alliance, and individual experience, but these elements are not operationalized in the review
conceptual_tensions_4: Statistical significance in pain is separated from clinical relevance because the ETP pain effect did not exceed the MCID
conceptual_tensions_5: High heterogeneity and incomplete intervention reporting limit the review's ability to test dose-response or biopsychosocial mechanisms
additional_observations_1: The BPS label is used mainly as a concluding rationale for individualized exercise, not as an operational model for social variables
additional_observations_2: Psychosocial variables are secondary outcomes, and PCS and TSK are scarcely reported
additional_observations_3: The Pain Monitoring Model is used only to categorize baseline pain intensity for subgroup analysis
additional_observations_4: The Fitness-Fatigue model is invoked only to interpret delayed maximal strength effects
additional_observations_5: Language restrictions and RCT filters may limit generalizability
synthesis_note: This review uses BPS mainly as a concluding rationale for individualized, contextually framed exercise. It operationalizes biology through load-related physical outcomes and psychology through a few psychosocial measures; social content is named but not measured. Integration is strongest for load as graded exposure affecting fear and beliefs, with social factors only loosely attached.
coding_rationale: Bio-dominant because outcomes are load, pain, disability, endurance, and strength. Psychosocial content is measured but sparse; social content is named only. BPS integration is partial, not triadic.

citation: Gromakovskis (2025), Frontiers in Pain Research
title: Exploring fascia in myofascial pain syndrome: an integrative model of mechanisms
authors: Vlodeks Gromakovskis
pain_condition_detail: Myofascial pain syndrome (MPS), described as localized or regional pain with taut bands and myofascial trigger points reproducing referred pain when palpated.
context_note: Paper references the general population, specialized pain clinics, chronic low back and neck pain, and international initiatives for consensus terminology.
bps_function_set: explanatory framework; intervention rationale; operational definition; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses BPS mainly as an organizing and explanatory frame for a fascia-centered MPS model. It lists fascia, muscle, neural, and psychosocial factors, then links some through peripheral input, central sensitization, neuroimmune pathways, and multimodal treatment. It does not provide formal BPS definitions or operationalized variables.
integration_mechanism_summary: The main mechanism is peripheral-to-central: fascial densification, fibrosis, and inflammation generate nociceptive input, which contributes to peripheral sensitization, central sensitization, dorsal horn hyperexcitability, descending control changes, and cortical reorganization. Psychosocial factors are said to amplify pain through neuroimmune and central pathways, but no detailed psychosocial mechanism is specified.
quality_assessment_tools_1: sanra (scale for the assessment of narrative review articles)
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper argues for fascia as a central peripheral driver while also insisting that fascia should not be viewed in isolation
conceptual_tensions_2: It uses a biopsychosocial frame but gives much more substantive attention to fascia and central sensitization than to social factors
conceptual_tensions_3: It proposes psychosocial factors amplify pain through neuroimmune and central pathways but does not elaborate the psychosocial mechanism
conceptual_tensions_4: It criticizes muscle-centric and central sensitization models as incomplete, while proposing fascia as a unifying substrate that may risk reductionism if psychosocial domains are ignored
additional_observations_1: The article is a conceptual narrative review, not a systematic review or meta-analysis, despite searching PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Google Scholar
additional_observations_2: The review's most concrete operationalization is a named integrative conceptual model with fascial pathology, muscular dysfunction, central sensitization, and psychosocial influences
additional_observations_3: Psychological and social constructs are named but not measured, defined, or linked to specific instruments
additional_observations_4: The social domain is essentially collapsed into psychosocial factors, with no named social determinants such as work, family, healthcare access, or socioeconomic position
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS as a fascia-centered explanatory frame for MPS. Biological content is rich and sustained, especially fascia, nociception, inflammation, mechanotransduction, and central sensitization. Psychological content is present but mostly listed and undifferentiated. Social content is thin and underexplored. The paper proposes peripheral-to-central and neuroimmune pathways, but triadic integration remains partial rather than a fully specified three-domain mechanism.
coding_rationale: Bio-dominant pseudo-BPS: BPS is used analytically to organize fascia, muscle, neural, and psychosocial content, but social factors are minimally specified and triadic integration is mostly parallel with some peripheral-to-central mechanisms.

title: Social factors contributing to the development of chronic low back pain: a scoping review
authors: Yvan Sonjon; Annabelle Gonthier; Camille Lépingle; Jean-Baptiste Van der Henst; Karen T. Reilly; Eric Chabanat
pain_condition_detail: Adult non-specific chronic low back pain (CLBP), defined as lumbar pain for at least 3 months after acute causes/treatments have been addressed.
context_note: Industrialized Western countries with comparable relational, cultural, political frameworks and healthcare structures/delivery models; WEIRD limitation noted.
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; justification; operational definition; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: It uses BPS chiefly to define social factors as external influences and to classify 28 categories into six domains. Biological and psychological factors are included only when socially shaped; pairwise pathways are cited, but no triadic mechanism is modeled.
integration_mechanism_summary: No three-domain mechanism proposed. It proposes social determinants shaping lifestyle/health indicators and stigma affecting care access, and psychosocial mediators such as depression and perceived stress linking social conditions to pain outcomes; biological, psychological, and social factors are not modeled as a single system.

emergent_labels_9: MacArthur Scale of Subjective Social Status
emergent_labels_12: health literacy specific to low back pain
conceptual_tensions_1: BPS is used to justify social-factor inclusion, but the review’s own synthesis is mainly descriptive classification rather than mechanism
conceptual_tensions_2: Biological or psychological factors are reclassified as social when socially shaped, creating a debatable boundary between domains
conceptual_tensions_3: Social relationships are described as important for recovery, yet family and professional support remain underexplored
conceptual_tensions_4: Social factors are often treated as adjustment variables or economic impacts rather than explanatory contributors to CLBP progression
conceptual_tensions_5: Western WEIRD restriction may underrepresent marginalized populations and systemic or cultural injustice
additional_observations_1: The review explicitly states that included studies used a BPS model, but its own synthesis is a descriptive classification of social factors
additional_observations_2: No critical appraisal or risk-of-bias assessment was conducted because the authors judged it inappropriate for the scoping-review aim
additional_observations_3: The review says its reclassification of biological or psychological factors as social is descriptive and does not reinterpret original findings
additional_observations_4: The paper recommends mixed methods and participatory action research for underrepresented domains
additional_observations_5: The review calls for hypothesis-driven research to test temporal and potentially causal links between social factors and CLBP evolution
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS mainly as a social lens for CLBP. It elaborates social and psychosocial factors, mentions biological/lifestyle factors when socially shaped, and uses BPS to justify classification and care strategies. It names pairwise pathways, especially social-psychological mediators, but does not model a three-domain system.
coding_rationale: Social-dominant pseudo-BPS: BPS organizes the review and care rationale, but biological content is thin and triadic integration is absent.

citation: Potthoff et al. (2025), International Journal for Equity in Health
title: Social dimensions as explanatory approaches for the development of chronic pain: a meta-ethnography of qualitative studies
authors: Sarah Potthoff; Dominik Koesling; Claudia Bozzaro
journal: International Journal for Equity in Health
pain_condition_detail: Chronic non-malignant pain, especially chronic low back pain and headache disorders.
context_note: Worldwide studies; most in Anglo-American countries, with migration, refugee history, and disadvantaged neighborhoods as recurring contexts.
bps_function_set: background framing; critique or problematization; explanatory framework; justification; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses BPS mainly as a critique: it names biomedical, psychological, and social etiologies but operationalizes the review by excluding psychosocial-only studies and synthesizing social dimensions. Biological and psychological content appear as background/context, not integrated mechanisms.
integration_mechanism_summary: Social-to-psychological mechanisms dominate: stigma and gendered expectations can delay care, high expectations create stress and insufficient recovery, cultural stoicism delays treatment, and collectivist priorities reduce adherence. Trauma is framed as triggering pain and mental health consequences; biomedical content is mostly background.
quality_assessment_tools_1: jbi critical appraisal checklist for qualitative research
emergent_labels_3: critical theoretical understanding of the social
emergent_labels_4: gender as a category that primarily refers to biological sex
emergent_labels_6: stigmatization, discrimination, and marginalization based on social identity
emergent_labels_8: high expectations regarding work or school
emergent_labels_9: cultural and religious beliefs and values
conceptual_tensions_1: BPS is presented as biomedical, psychological, and social, yet the review argues that prior BPS-oriented research has neglected the social
conceptual_tensions_2: The social is criticized for being subsumed under psychosocial and psychological meanings, but the review still uses psychological constructs within social explanations
conceptual_tensions_3: Quantitative social-factor studies are said to be limited because they focus on objective, measurable factors rather than subtle interactions and patient experience
conceptual_tensions_4: Gender is treated both as biological sex and as gender relations/social inequality, and the review privileges the latter
conceptual_tensions_5: The review excludes studies that discuss the social merely as an individual psychosocial phenomenon, so psychological material appears but is not analyzed as a psychological domain
additional_observations_1: The review’s inclusion criteria explicitly excluded studies that discussed the social merely as an individual psychosocial phenomenon from a psychological perspective
additional_observations_2: The paper states that it focused exclusively on study results related to social dimensions and did not analyze additional results from included studies
additional_observations_3: Included studies were worldwide but concentrated in Anglo-American countries, English and German language limits are named as limitations
additional_observations_4: Implications include social workers in medical teams, gender and discrimination sensitivity training, childcare options, poverty programs, housing, secure jobs, and health infrastructure
additional_observations_5: The paper treats lifestyle factors as an eighth social dimension rather than as a separate lifestyle framework
synthesis_note: This paper contributes a rich social-domain ontology of chronic pain development but not a biopsychosocial integration model. It operationalizes BPS by critiquing the neglect of social dimensions and synthesizing eight social categories; biomedical and psychological content remain background rather than mechanistically integrated.
coding_rationale: Social content is elaborated; bio, psych, and lifestyle are mentioned. BPS is used critically to justify a social-domain review, not as a three-domain mechanism.

citation: Rinaudo et al. (2025), PLOS One
title: Navigating the biopsychosocial landscape: A systematic review on the association between social support and chronic pain
authors: Carlo Matej Rinaudo; Maxim Van de Velde; Arnaud Steyaert; André Mouraux; Bianka Karshikoff
pain_condition_detail: Chronic pain (persistent or recurrent pain lasting longer than 3 months), including musculoskeletal pain, fibromyalgia, spinal cord injury, neurological/neuromuscular pain or disability, chronic migraine/headache, post-surgical pain, chronic pelvic pain, articular pain, and unspecified chronic pain.
context_note: Studies were mainly conducted in the USA, Canada or Europe; only three studies were outside these regions (South Korea and Australia); authors note Western-country generalisability limits.
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; justification
bps_operationalization_summary: The review uses BPS mainly to justify a social-support focus, then operationalizes only social support (PSS, SSS, SpR) and compares them with pain, QoL, depression, and anxiety outcomes. It does not code or model biological, psychological, and social domains as an integrated system.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes a social-support pathway in which support buffers stress through stress appraisal and active coping, potentially reducing pain; spousal responses may reinforce pain behaviour through operant learning. It does not specify a full three-domain mechanism in which biological, psychological, and social factors reciprocally shape one another.
quality_assessment_tools_1: adapted version of the “jbi critical appraisal checklist for analytical cross-sectional studies”
quality_assessment_tools_3: adapted version of the quality assessment tool of hawker et al
emergent_labels_11: operant conditioning theory of chronic pain
conceptual_tensions_1: The BPS label frames chronic pain as biological, psychological, and social, but the review’s operational exposure is social support rather than all three domains
conceptual_tensions_2: Social support generally appears beneficial, but spousal responses can be associated with worse pain, disability, and depression
conceptual_tensions_3: The evidence base is mostly cross-sectional and correlational, yet the paper discusses possible causality and future longitudinal designs
conceptual_tensions_4: Different social support constructs and questionnaires create inconsistency and obscure whether PSS, SSS, and SpR have comparable meanings
conceptual_tensions_5: Spousal responses are explicitly not a measure of social support per se, yet they are included as an important chronic-pain social factor
additional_observations_1: The review does not perform meta-analysis, it uses vote counting and correlation/regression direction because of heterogeneity and lack of effect sizes
additional_observations_2: No included studies were randomized, and only eight of 40 final studies were longitudinal
additional_observations_3: Spousal responses are treated as a social exposure because they influence pain behaviour and well-being, even though the paper says they are not social support per se
additional_observations_4: The paper’s closest triadic mechanism is stress-buffering through stress appraisal and active coping, but it is not tied to a full BPS operational model
additional_observations_5: Biological content is concentrated in pain/nociception definitions and pain outcomes rather than mechanisms such as inflammation, genetics, imaging, or peripheral sensitization
additional_observations_6: The conclusion recommends spouse education and including spouses in treatment sessions, which turns social support findings into applied pain-management suggestions
synthesis_note: This review uses a BPS-labeled title/intro but operationalizes social support rather than the full BPS model. It codes PSS, SSS, and SpR against pain, QoL, depression, and anxiety, mostly with cross-sectional correlations. It offers stress-buffering and operant-learning pathways but no full biological-psychological-social system.
coding_rationale: Social support dominates; psychological outcomes are developed; biological content is limited to pain/nociception. BPS frames the topic but does not create a triadic mechanism, so pseudo_bps/partial integration.

citation: Tjell et al. (2025), Frontiers in Neurology
title: Poly-symptomatology of chronic multi-canalicular benign paroxysmal positional vertigo: a deductive, inductive, and abductive narrative review
authors: Carsten Tjell; Wenche Iglebekk; Peter Borenstein
pain_condition_detail: Chronic multi-canalicular benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (mc-BPPV), with symptoms overlapping vestibular migraine, WAD, ME/CFS, and other chronic pain disorders.
bps_function_set: background framing; critique or problematization; rhetorical label
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper operationalizes chronic mc-BPPV through vestibular anatomy, otolith/cupula mechanisms, vestibular nuclei reflexes, and symptom frequencies. The BPS label is not operationalized as measured domains.
integration_mechanism_summary: Vestibular-to-neural reflex pathways are proposed for cognitive, postural, neck, and other symptoms; no biological-psychological-social mechanism is proposed.
pain_conditions_1: chronic multi-canalicular benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (mc-bppv)
emergent_labels_1: chronic multi-canalicular benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (mc-BPPV)
conceptual_tensions_1: The article treats BPPV as benign and paroxysmal while focusing on chronic multi-canalicular presentations
conceptual_tensions_2: The BPS label is used to critique misclassification, but the review's own causal account is vestibular-biological
conceptual_tensions_3: Many symptom links are deductive, inductive, or abductive, with abductive sections relying on personal experience and uncertainty
conceptual_tensions_4: Symptoms overlap with vestibular migraine, ME/CFS, WAD, and Menière's disease, making attribution difficult
conceptual_tensions_5: The review narrows objective findings to vestibular findings rather than treating lack of findings as lack of findings generally
additional_observations_1: The paper's evidence synthesis method is deductive, inductive, and abductive rather than a BPS domain matrix
additional_observations_2: The Dizziness Handicap Inventory is the only named patient-reported outcome instrument
additional_observations_3: Psychological content is limited to cognitive/affective states, anxiety, stress, frustration, and quality of life
additional_observations_4: Social content is limited to diagnosis, clinicians, physiotherapy clinics, and multiple specialists
additional_observations_5: The BPS label appears only in the abstract and introduction
additional_observations_6: The review does not report a formal risk-of-bias or quality assessment tool for included studies
synthesis_note: This review uses BPS language to argue that chronic mc-BPPV symptoms are mislabeled psychosocial when vestibular findings are absent. Its operational content is vestibular neurophysiology and symptom attribution; psychological and social material is incidental. It does not develop a three-domain model or mechanism.
coding_rationale: BPS is explicit but undefined and only rhetorical/critical. Biology dominates; psych/social are thin. Triadic integration is partial because diagnostic context and affective responses are present but not mechanistically linked.

title: A debate on integrative vs . interventional approaches to chronic pain: does telemedicine play a role?
authors: Kush Patel; Leena Mathew; Alopi Patel
pain_condition_detail: Chronic pain in general, with examples including spinal pain, osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, chronic lower back pain, fibromyalgia, migraines, and neurodegenerative disease.
context_note: Discusses Western medicine, insurance coverage, rural access, socioeconomic inequities, and access to healthy foods or safe exercise environments.
bps_function_set: background framing; intervention rationale; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses the BPS label to frame chronic pain as biological, psychological, and socio-environmental, but operationalizes the argument mainly through lifestyle medicine pillars, telemedicine access, and barriers to implementation rather than measuring or modeling domain interactions.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes biological and psychological mechanisms for nutrition, stress, sleep, substances, and exercise, and social mechanisms for support, access, and healthcare systems. It does not specify a full three-domain pathway in which biological, psychological, and social factors act on one another as a single system.
conceptual_tensions_1: The article frames pain as biopsychosocial but operationalizes most of the argument through lifestyle medicine, telemedicine access, and reimbursement barriers
conceptual_tensions_2: Integrative care is presented as comprehensive, while interventional pain medicine is justified by anatomical and neurochemical pathways and rapid analgesia
conceptual_tensions_3: Lifestyle medicine is described as evidence-based and beneficial, but constrained by time, training, adherence, resources, and insurance coverage
conceptual_tensions_4: Telemedicine is presented as a solution to time and access barriers but itself has technical, physical-exam, tool-access, and security limitations
conceptual_tensions_5: The paper names future outcome measures but does not specify instruments or validated measures for the constructs it discusses
additional_observations_1: The article is a debate rather than a systematic review or empirical study, so no quality assessment or risk-of-bias tools are reported
additional_observations_2: The paper’s strongest integration is within the biological-psychological interface, especially stress, sleep, inflammation, and substance use
additional_observations_3: Social content is substantial but mainly concerns access, support, insurance, reimbursement, policy, and telemedicine, not interpersonal mechanisms in pain care
additional_observations_4: The paper treats telemedicine as an implementation infrastructure rather than as a psychological, biological, or social construct
synthesis_note: This paper uses the biopsychosocial label to justify lifestyle medicine for chronic pain, but its substantive content is dominated by lifestyle, biomedical, and healthcare-system factors. Psychological content appears mainly as stress, anxiety, fatigue, mental health, adherence, and behavioral change. It offers some biological-psychological and social-psychological pathways, but not a full three-domain mechanism.
coding_rationale: BPS is explicit but mostly organizational. Lifestyle medicine supplies the operational content, with elaborated biological, lifestyle, and social domains, mentioned psychological content, and partial triadic integration.

title: Chronic pain in European adult populations: a systematic review of prevalence and associated clinical features
authors: Caroline Rometsch; Alexandra Martin; Florian Junne; Fiammetta Cosci
pain_condition_detail: Chronic pain in European adults, assessed as point, period, and lifetime prevalence across body locations including headaches, neck/shoulder, back, abdomen, hip, arm/wrist/ankle, leg/knee, chest/stomach, and lower extremities.
context_note: European adult general population; prevalence data from EU countries including Austria, Belgium, Finland, France, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Italy, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, The Netherlands, and United Kingdom, with many missing countries.
bps_function_set: intervention rationale; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The review uses BPS only in the abstract and discussion to justify comprehensive, multimodal care. The review itself stratifies prevalence by sociodemographic and clinical features and conducts meta-regression on sex, marital status, and employment, not as variables in a BPS model.
integration_mechanism_summary: No three-domain mechanism is proposed. The only named mediator is pain interference linking CP severity to affect and quality of life; otherwise domains are associated, listed, or used to justify comprehensive care.
quality_assessment_tools_1: joanna biggs institutes' critical appraisal checklist for studies reporting prevalence data (jbi)
emergent_labels_4: International Association for the Study of Pain
emergent_labels_7: Joanna Biggs Institutes' Critical Appraisal Checklist for Studies Reporting Prevalence Data (JBI)
conceptual_tensions_1: The review invokes a comprehensive BPS model but does not define it or use it to select, measure, or model variables
conceptual_tensions_2: Prevalence heterogeneity is attributed to diagnostic criteria, cutoffs, and assessment tools, yet these sources of variation are not modeled
conceptual_tensions_3: Narrative associations between sociodemographic features and CP are not statistically significant in meta-regression
conceptual_tensions_4: European coverage is uneven, with many countries explicitly listed as missing despite the review's European scope
conceptual_tensions_5: The discussion broadens from BPS to psychosomatic medicine, clinimetrics, macro-analysis, and Whipple's principle without resolving the BPS operational gap
additional_observations_1: The meta-regression operationalizes sociodemographic moderators only as sex, marital status, and employment status
additional_observations_2: Quality assessment focused on prevalence-study methods rather than BPS construct validity
additional_observations_3: SF-36 was the only named patient-reported outcome instrument in the evidence
additional_observations_4: Psychosomatic medicine, clinimetrics, macro-analysis, and Whipple's principle extend the care rationale beyond BPS
additional_observations_5: Environmental factors are named but not operationalized
additional_observations_6: Pain location and regional pain burden are the main biological operationalization
synthesis_note: This review operationalizes BPS only as a rationale for comprehensive, multimodal care after a prevalence-focused synthesis. It names biological, psychological, and social correlates but treats them mainly as associated features, with no substantive three-domain model or measured BPS variables.
coding_rationale: Multifactorial: all domains are named, but BPS is used mainly for care recommendations. Triadic integration is descriptive only; no three-domain mechanism is modeled.

citation: Monroe et al. (2025), The journal of pain
title: Psychologically Informed Physical Therapy Management of Chronic Musculoskeletal Pain in Culturally Diverse Populations: An Intervention Logic Model
authors: Katrina S. Monroe; Kristin R. Archer; Stephen T. Wegener; Sara P. Gombatto
pain_condition_detail: Chronic musculoskeletal pain; examples include low back pain, neck pain, and chronic spine pain.
context_note: Illustration focuses on US Hispanic/Latino persons seeking care for chronic spine pain at a Federally Qualified Health Center near the United States-Mexico border; broader context includes CALD populations and low- and middle-income nations.
bps_function_set: background framing; critique or problematization; intervention rationale; justification; operational definition; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper turns the BPS frame into a PIPT logic model: cognitive skill training plus aerobic activity, therapeutic exercise, and graded functional movement. It specifies determinants such as psychological flexibility, self-efficacy, catastrophizing, fear, and pain beliefs, and tailors them to sociocultural factors such as language, health literacy, familismo, personalismo, and social support.
integration_mechanism_summary: PIPT combines cognitive skill training with aerobic activity, therapeutic exercise, and graded functional movement. The proposed pathway is active cognitive and physical coping behaviors, mediated by psychological flexibility, self-efficacy, reduced catastrophizing/fear/maladaptive beliefs, leading to less pain/disability and greater work/social participation. Sociocultural factors are proposed as moderators/mediators and tailoring guides, not a fully specified three-domain mechanism.
emergent_labels_12: Medical Outcomes Study Social Support Measure
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper critiques existing biopsychosocial/PIPT frameworks for missing socioeconomic, ethnocultural, and interpersonal factors while proposing a PIPT model that remains centered on physical therapy interventions
conceptual_tensions_2: The general model is grounded in PIPT evidence, yet the authors state that mediators may differ in CALD populations and must be tested
conceptual_tensions_3: Social factors are central to tailoring and proposed as mediators/moderators, but the core mechanism remains primarily cognitive-emotional and physical
conceptual_tensions_4: The paper calls for culturally relevant care while acknowledging that existing rehabilitation frameworks are vague, difficult to test, and limited to behavioral mechanisms

additional_observations_2: The Latino example is operationalized in a Federally Qualified Health Center near the United States-Mexico border
additional_observations_3: The social domain is more developed than in many PIPT papers but functions mainly as tailoring, moderator, mediator, and contextual determinant
additional_observations_4: The paper does not provide formal definitions for most psychological constructs beyond psychological flexibility

synthesis_note: The paper operationalizes BPS as a PIPT logic model: physical therapy components plus cognitive-emotional skill training plus sociocultural tailoring. It goes beyond listing domains by specifying mediators/moderators and culturally relevant constructs, but the social domain mainly functions as context/tailoring for a biopsychosocial PIPT mechanism rather than as an independently modeled causal system.
coding_rationale: All three domains are present and linked, but the social domain is mostly a moderator/tailoring layer; therefore triadic integration is partial rather than a fully specified three-way mechanism.

title: The potential impact of exercise on affect and neuroinflammation in older adults living with fibromyalgia: a scoping review
authors: Taylor L. Taylor; Fitzgerald Dodds; McKenna Tharpe; Emily L. Zumbro; Michael Hankes; Raymond Jones; Deanna Rumble; Lisa Antoine; Kristen Allen-Watts; Andrew Sims; Reshu Chandra; Burel R. Goodin; Jarred Younger; Thomas W. Buford
pain_condition_detail: Fibromyalgia (FM); eligibility allowed FM-related Chronic Fatigue Syndrome, but extracted study characteristics state all studies evaluated exercise in FM samples.
context_note: NIA Health Disparities Framework highlights geographic/political factors, cultural factors, coping factors, and physiological indicators as pain research priorities.
bps_function_set: background framing; intervention rationale; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper operationalizes BPS as exercise plus affect and neuroinflammation outcomes, with adherence and social barriers as context; it does not define the model or assign coded variables to all three domains.
integration_mechanism_summary: Proposed pathway: exercise changes affect and inflammatory/neuroinflammatory markers; cytokines/microglia/BBB link inflammation to dysregulated affect and pain; affect changes and neuroinflammation may improve adherence. Social factors are barriers/context, not part of the pathway.
conceptual_tensions_1: The review proposes neuroinflammation/affect mechanisms while stating evidence is limited and attribution speculative
conceptual_tensions_2: Exercise is framed as beneficial, yet acute bouts can worsen pain/fatigue and drive fear avoidance/adherence problems
conceptual_tensions_3: The review focuses on older adults but notes many included participants were young and middle-aged adults
conceptual_tensions_4: Social factors are invoked through barriers and disparities but are not measured or integrated into the main mechanism
conceptual_tensions_5: Scoping review methods included all available literature and did not weight conclusions by quality despite risk-of-bias assessments
additional_observations_1: No named psychological or social instruments are used, outcomes are reported as study outcomes
additional_observations_2: The conceptual framework is central but is proposed for future testing rather than tested in this review
additional_observations_3: The paper treats exercise as both lifestyle behavior and intervention component
additional_observations_4: It distinguishes neuroinflammation from systemic inflammation but uses both in mechanisms
additional_observations_5: It calls for qualitative approaches to exercise adherence
additional_observations_6: Quality assessments were conducted but not weighted in the scoping review synthesis
synthesis_note: The review operationalizes BPS mainly through exercise, affect, neuroinflammation, and adherence in older adults with FM. It develops biological and psychological mechanisms while social factors remain barriers/context, yielding partial BPS integration.
coding_rationale: Bio and psych are elaborated; social is thin. BPS label organizes the review and supports exercise rationale, but no model definition or full triadic integration is provided.

citation: Cardoso et al. (2024), Interactive Journal of Medical Research
title: Wearable Devices for Supporting Chronic Disease Self-Management: Scoping Review
authors: Taiane de Azevedo Cardoso; Jari Ruokolainen; Wentao Wang; Marie-Pierre Gagnon; Steven Ouellet; Eugène Attisso; Wilfried Supper; Samira Amil; Caroline Rhéaume; Jean-Sébastien Paquette; Christian Chabot; Marie-Claude Laferrière; Maxime Sasseville
pain_condition_detail: Chronic pain; musculoskeletal conditions (osteoporosis, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, ankylosing spondylitis); diabetes, heart failure, cardiovascular conditions, hypertension, COPD, asthma, and multimorbidity.
context_note: Most studies were in North America (United States and Canada), with smaller shares in the United Kingdom, Republic of Korea, China, Netherlands, Spain, and multi-country studies.
bps_function_set: conclusion; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper uses BPS as an outcome taxonomy, not a model. It classifies measured outcomes into clinical, behavioral, technology-experience, holistic/biopsychosocial, and health-care-system categories; it reports counts and significance but does not model mechanisms linking domains.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes a device-centered pathway: physiological data from wearables generate real-time feedback; feedback may be automatic or clinician-mediated; this promotes engagement/adherence to health behaviors and can enter clinical workflows. It does not propose a chronic-pain-specific biopsychosocial mechanism.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper uses a broad chronic-disease wearable frame while chronic pain is represented by only 6 of 79 studies
conceptual_tensions_2: The BPS label is used to describe outcome categories, but no formal biopsychosocial model or chronic-pain mechanism is provided
conceptual_tensions_3: The review reports measured outcomes and effect direction but does not consider effect sizes
conceptual_tensions_4: Multicomponent behavioral strategy interventions are acknowledged as confounding factors but not considered
conceptual_tensions_5: MMAT quality assessment is reported, but no studies are excluded based on MMAT scores
additional_observations_1: Chronic pain studies used only wearable activity trackers and reported clinical, behavioral, and technology-experience outcomes
additional_observations_2: Most included studies were conducted in North America, especially the United States
additional_observations_3: Wearable activity trackers were the most common device across the review
additional_observations_4: The paper's BPS-related content appears mainly in outcome categorization rather than in chronic-pain theory
additional_observations_5: The review includes chronic disease self-management broadly, not only pain populations
additional_observations_6: Quality assessment was performed, but methodological rigor did not determine inclusion
synthesis_note: This paper contributes a scoping map of wearable-device interventions across chronic diseases, with chronic pain as a small cluster. It operationalizes BPS only by adding a holistic/biopsychosocial outcome category; it does not define the model or propose chronic-pain-specific mechanisms. Most evidence is clinical/behavioral, with social content limited to health-care system outcomes.
coding_rationale: BPS is used as an outcome taxonomy across chronic diseases, not a chronic-pain BPS model. Bio and psych outcomes dominate; social appears mainly as health-care system outcomes. Integration is device-feedback rather than three-domain chronic-pain mechanism.

title: Same patient but different worlds: A state-of-the-art review translating best practice psychosocial care from musculoskeletal care to the orthopaedic context
authors: Marie K. March; Katharine E. Roberts
pain_condition_detail: Persistent/chronic musculoskeletal conditions in elective orthopaedic surgery, informed by musculoskeletal care.
context_note: Elective orthopaedic secondary care in hospital settings, with implementation lessons from primary-care musculoskeletal care and attention to women, culturally diverse and low-literacy communities.
bps_function_set: background framing; explanatory framework; intervention rationale; justification; organizing principle; policy or practice implication
bps_operationalization_summary: The paper operationalizes BPS mainly by translating psychosocial assessment, screening tools, interventions, workforce training, shared decision making, registries and equity implementation into orthopaedic care. It lists biological, psychological and social predictors but does not specify a three-domain mechanism.
integration_mechanism_summary: No detailed cross-domain mechanisms are proposed. The paper mainly states that biological, psychological and social factors predict poor recovery and that psychosocial assessment and intervention should be implemented in orthopaedics; the closest pathway is psychosocial assessment/intervention affecting outcomes.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper says BPS requires interaction of physical, emotional and social factors, but the substantive review is mainly psychosocial implementation with biological factors mostly listed
conceptual_tensions_2: Screening tools for psychosocial risk are recommended in musculoskeletal care, yet orthopaedics lacks a universal comprehensive patient interview incorporating a biopsychosocial approach
conceptual_tensions_3: Decision aids are presented as shared decision-making tools, but the paper says decision aids without interactive processes have not improved surgical outcomes
conceptual_tensions_4: Multidisciplinary mental health care is recommended, but workforce costs and funding models are barriers
conceptual_tensions_5: Equity is emphasized for women and culturally diverse communities, but the paper says these groups have been excluded from research previously
additional_observations_1: The article is a state-of-the-art implementation review, not an effectiveness synthesis of BPS interventions
additional_observations_2: It uses primary-care musculoskeletal evidence to infer what orthopaedic surgery should implement
additional_observations_3: It treats psychosocial assessment as a screening and implementation task rather than as a validated three-domain model
additional_observations_4: Registry datasets are proposed as infrastructure for standardized psychosocial measurement
additional_observations_5: The paper foregrounds equity through women, ethnic minorities, language, literacy, and socio-gendered inequity
additional_observations_6: It mentions paediatric and adult cancer care only as analogies for implementation complexity
synthesis_note: This review uses the BPS label mainly to justify implementation of psychosocial assessment and care in orthopaedics. It lists biological, psychological and social predictors of poor recovery, but the analytic work is in psychosocial screening, interventions, workforce and implementation systems. It offers descriptive triadic linkage rather than a three-domain mechanism.
coding_rationale: BPS functions mainly as intervention rationale and organizing principle. Psychosocial and social content are elaborated, biology is mentioned, and triadic integration is descriptive only.

title: What are the functional and clinical characteristics shared by fibromyalgia and low back pain? A scoping review
authors: Bastien Couëpel; Mathieu Tremblay; Marjorie Bernier; Jacques Abboud; Martin Descarreaux
pain_condition_detail: fibromyalgia and chronic primary/non-specific low back pain
context_note: Included studies covered multiple countries; review restricted to English/French publications and three databases.
bps_function_set: background framing; justification; organizing principle
bps_operationalization_summary: BPS label is used to frame burden and organize comparison across pain-related, physiological, and psychological outcomes; the review does not define or model interactions among domains.
integration_mechanism_summary: The paper proposes psychological symptoms may contribute to central sensitization, central sensitization may predict widespread pain, and the relation with widespread pain may be bidirectional. No social-domain pathway is proposed.
conceptual_tensions_1: The paper uses biopsychosocial burden while leaving the model undefined and unmechanized
conceptual_tensions_2: LBP definitions are inconsistent across included studies
conceptual_tensions_3: ACR criteria differ across studies and may select more severe FM cases
conceptual_tensions_4: Measurement heterogeneity and missing minimal clinically important differences limit synthesis
conceptual_tensions_5: The proposed psychological-to-widespread-pain pathway is explicitly bidirectional and unknown
additional_observations_1: No formal risk-of-bias or quality appraisal of included studies is reported
additional_observations_2: Included study designs were mostly cross-sectional, limiting claims about progression from LBP to FM
additional_observations_3: The search was restricted to English/French publications and three databases
additional_observations_4: The social domain appears mainly as social support and socioeconomic descriptors, not as a modeled determinant
synthesis_note: The paper operationalizes BPS as a comparative framework rather than an integrated explanatory model. Biological and psychological mechanisms are discussed, especially central sensitization and affect/cognition, but social content is reduced to socioeconomic context and social support.
coding_rationale: Bio and psych are elaborated; social is mentioned. Bio-psych integration is mechanistic; triadic integration is partial because social factors are not tied into the mechanism. Typology is multifactorial.
